tasks.prompt: Order an ultraviolet sleeve cleaning program for a hard water plant.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional ultraviolet plant in Alberta with mineral scale forming on lamp sleeves.
tasks.configuration: Scope: fouling rate measured through a cleaning interval program in service.

cards.label: Measure intensity loss between cleanings and inspect a sleeve to confirm mineral scale as the cause
Select the mechanical wiping or chemical cleaning method approved for the reactor and water chemistry
Clean one reactor and measure intensity recovery at reference conditions
Set the cleaning interval from the measured fouling rate with margin before the dose limit is reached
Run the interval program for two cycles and compare intensity trends with the baseline
File the cleaning method, interval, and recovery records in the ultraviolet program

tasks.explanation: The cleaning interval is set from measured fouling rate and proven recovery, so sleeves are cleaned before scale can pull dose below target.

tasks.prompt: Order the ultraviolet dose monitoring and reporting routine for compliance records.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional senior operator in western Canada building the monthly ultraviolet record for provincial reporting in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: daily dose data through the filed monthly summary.

cards.label: Collect daily flow, transmittance, intensity, and calculated dose for every duty reactor
Flag every period when dose fell below the required value or a reactor ran outside its validated range
Check flagged periods against operator logs for the action taken and the duration
Calculate the share of treated volume that received full required dose for the month
Summarize alarms, lamp changes, and cleanings that explain the flagged periods
File the monthly summary and carry any unresolved dose gap into the corrective action list

tasks.explanation: The monthly record pairs dose data with the operator log, so every low dose period carries its cause, duration, and action rather than standing unexplained.

tasks.prompt: Order a combined ultraviolet and chlorine credit management program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional plant in Saskatchewan claiming ultraviolet credit for one organism group and chlorine contact credit for another.
tasks.configuration: Scope: credit split defined through combined credit verified at worst case conditions.

cards.label: Record which inactivation credit each barrier provides and the conditions each credit requires
Set ultraviolet dose and chlorine residual and contact time targets that together meet the total requirement
Identify the worst combined condition of cold water, low transmittance, and peak flow
Verify both barriers meet their targets at that condition using plant records or a controlled test
Set alarms so a shortfall in either barrier raises the other barrier review the same shift
File the combined credit program and brief all shifts on the paired targets

tasks.explanation: Credits are managed as a pair and verified at the worst combined condition, so neither barrier is allowed to drift on the assumption the other will cover it.

tasks.prompt: Order the ultraviolet reactor recommissioning after lamp and sensor replacement.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional ultraviolet reactor in Manitoba returning after major lamp and sensor replacement.
tasks.configuration: Scope: reactor opened for work through the reactor trusted for disinfection credit.

cards.label: Confirm replacement lamps, sleeves, and sensors match the validated reactor configuration
Calibrate the new intensity and transmittance sensors against reference instruments
Run the reactor across its flow range and compare delivered dose with the validated curve
Check dose pacing, alarms, and automatic controls at low, normal, and peak flow
Run the reactor in parallel duty for one week and trend dose against the other reactors
Accept the reactor for credit, file new baselines, and update the maintenance record

tasks.explanation: A rebuilt reactor is recommissioned against its validated curve and trended beside its peers for a week before its dose is trusted for credit again.

tasks.prompt: Order an ultraviolet advanced oxidation awareness study for taste and odour events.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional plant in Alberta studying ultraviolet with an oxidant for seasonal taste and odour compounds.
tasks.configuration: Scope: event characterization through a decision on advanced oxidation adoption.

cards.label: Characterize the taste and odour events by compound indicator, raw concentration pattern, and duration
Review bench or pilot results for ultraviolet dose and oxidant dose needed to reduce the compounds
Check effects on disinfection credit, byproduct indicators, and downstream chlorine demand
Trial the process at plant scale during the next event at the studied doses
Compare treated taste and odour results and customer complaints with previous events
Decide adoption from the trial evidence and file the study with operating limits if adopted

tasks.explanation: Advanced oxidation is adopted only after a plant scale event trial shows compound reduction without costing disinfection credit or creating new quality problems.

tasks.prompt: Order the winter ultraviolet operating program for a cold climate plant.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional ultraviolet plant in northern Saskatchewan operating through extreme cold.
tasks.configuration: Scope: cold risks reviewed through winter settings and checks in service.

cards.label: List cold risks: lamp start reliability, sensor drift, frozen sample lines, and building heat loss
Confirm lamp warm up and restart behaviour at winter building temperatures with the supplier program
Protect and heat trace sample and drain lines and test alarms for low building temperature
Increase intensity and dose verification checks through the coldest month
Stage spare lamps, sleeves, and ballasts on site for the winter period
Record winter performance and set the spring review of cold related faults

tasks.explanation: Winter operation protects the supporting systems, lines, heat, and spares, and increases dose verification when cold makes every fault harder to reach and fix.

tasks.prompt: Order the ultraviolet sensor calibration and verification program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional ultraviolet plant in British Columbia setting a standing sensor verification routine.
tasks.configuration: Scope: reference instruments confirmed through routine verifications trended.

cards.label: Confirm reference intensity and transmittance instruments are themselves calibrated and in date
Compare each duty sensor with its reference at the program interval under stable reactor conditions
Adjust or replace any sensor outside the program tolerance and record the as found error
Check dose calculation after any sensor change at reference flow and transmittance
Trend as found errors to set which sensors need shorter verification intervals
File calibration records by sensor and review the program annually

tasks.explanation: Sensor verification uses in date references, records as found error, and proves the dose calculation after every change, so dose records rest on trusted measurement.

tasks.prompt: Order the standby power test for ultraviolet disinfection continuity.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional plant in western Canada proving ultraviolet disinfection survives a power interruption.
tasks.configuration: Scope: test planned through disinfection continuity proven and filed.

cards.label: Plan the test at moderate flow with the clearwell level high enough to buffer a short interruption
Transfer the plant to standby power and record reactor behaviour, lamp restrike time, and dose recovery
Confirm automatic controls restart reactors in the correct order and alarms report the event
Measure how long treated flow ran below required dose, if at all, and the volume affected
Return to normal power, verify dose at reference conditions, and inspect lamps for restrike faults
File the test with restrike and recovery times and correct any continuity gap found

tasks.explanation: The test measures restrike and dose recovery time under real transfer, because disinfection continuity depends on those minutes, not on the generator starting alone.

tasks.prompt: Order the ultraviolet program review after a source water quality change.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional plant in Manitoba whose source transmittance and organics shifted after a watershed change.
tasks.configuration: Scope: source change measured through ultraviolet set points revised and proven.

cards.label: Compare current transmittance, colour, and organics with the values the ultraviolet program was set on
Check dose margin at peak flow using the new worst transmittance
Review lamp intensity and sleeve condition to separate source effects from equipment decline
Revise dose pacing, flow limits, or cleaning intervals to restore margin on the new source
Verify revised settings over one month of operation and trend dose compliance
File the review and set a source monitoring trigger for the next review

tasks.explanation: A source change voids old dose margins, so the review remeasures the source, separates equipment decline, and reproves margin at peak flow on the new water.

tasks.prompt: Order a whole plant water balance study for a regional treatment plant.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional regional plant in Alberta accounting for raw, treated, backwash, and waste flows.
tasks.configuration: Scope: meter inventory through a closed water balance with losses explained.

cards.label: List and verify every flow meter from raw intake to finished water and every waste stream
Total inflows, treated output, backwash, cleaning, and known uses over a closed balance month
Compare meter totals with reservoir and clearwell level changes for the same period
Investigate the largest gap first by meter check, level survey, or waste stream measurement
Correct meter errors or record the true unmetered use that explains the gap
Close the balance within the program tolerance and file the monthly balance routine

tasks.explanation: A water balance closes only when meter totals agree with storage changes, and the largest gap is investigated first rather than averaged away.

tasks.prompt: Order a solids mass balance across coagulation, clarification, and filtration.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional plant in Saskatchewan tracing solids from raw water to residuals handling.
tasks.configuration: Scope: solids inputs defined through solids outputs reconciled.

cards.label: Calculate solids entering from raw turbidity and from coagulant and other chemical additions
Measure solids removed in clarifier sludge and filter backwash over the balance period
Measure solids leaving in finished water and solids accumulated in basins
Compare total solids out and accumulated with total solids in for the period
Investigate any imbalance segment by segment, starting with the clarifier sludge measurement
File the balance method and set the routine balance period for the residuals program

tasks.explanation: Chemical additions create solids as surely as raw turbidity does, so the balance counts both inputs before judging clarifier or filter capture.

tasks.prompt: Order a chlorine balance study across treatment and clearwell storage.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional plant in Manitoba tracing chlorine dose, demand, decay, and finished residual.
tasks.configuration: Scope: dose points mapped through decay explained and set points revised.

cards.label: Map every chlorine dose point and measure dose, demand, and residual at each stage for one week
Calculate stage by stage chlorine loss and compare with temperature and organics at each stage
Identify the stage with the largest unexplained loss and check for dose point or mixing problems
Correct the stage problem, such as a poor mixing point or a decaying day tank solution
Repeat the stage measurements and confirm finished residual stability at the same dose
File revised dose point set points and the balance method for seasonal repeats

tasks.explanation: The chlorine balance works stage by stage, so a loss is fixed where it happens instead of raising the total dose to cover an unknown sink.

tasks.prompt: Order an optimization study for clarifier sludge withdrawal scheduling.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional plant in British Columbia with clarifiers alternately carrying high blankets and wasting watery sludge.
tasks.configuration: Scope: blanket pattern recorded through an adopted withdrawal schedule.

cards.label: Record blanket depth, sludge solids, and withdrawal volumes for each clarifier for one month
Relate blanket excursions to withdrawal timing, raw solids, and flow changes
Trial a depth triggered withdrawal schedule on one clarifier for two weeks
Compare blanket stability and sludge solids with the time based schedule on the other clarifier
Adopt the better schedule for all clarifiers and set blanket alarm depths
Trend sludge solids to the residuals program so downstream handling sees the change coming

tasks.explanation: Withdrawal is optimized on blanket depth evidence, and the winning schedule is the one that holds the blanket while sending thicker sludge downstream.

tasks.prompt: Order a filter backwash optimization study to cut wash water without losing cleaning.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Class 3 plant in Alberta using a large share of production for backwashing.
tasks.configuration: Scope: wash baseline through optimized wash settings proven over repeated runs.

cards.label: Record wash rate, duration, waste turbidity profile, and headloss recovery for representative filters
Shorten one wash phase at a time on a trial filter, starting with the phase whose waste runs clearest
Run three full filter runs at each trial setting and compare headloss recovery and effluent quality
Stop shortening when recovery or effluent quality first weakens and step back one setting
Adopt the last fully passing wash program for the fleet and update the wash sequence records
Trend wash water share of production monthly and file the study

tasks.explanation: Wash water is cut one phase at a time with recovery as the judge, so savings stop at the last setting that still fully cleans the bed.

tasks.prompt: Order a demand forecasting and production scheduling program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional regional plant in Saskatchewan scheduling production against storage and energy price periods.
tasks.configuration: Scope: demand pattern built through scheduled production in routine use.

cards.label: Build hourly and daily demand patterns from three years of finished flow and storage records
Identify peak, shoulder, and low demand periods and the storage swing available in each
Schedule major production and backwashing into low demand or lower energy cost periods where quality allows
Set clearwell and reservoir level targets for the start of each demand period
Run the schedule for one month and compare storage, quality, and energy results with the previous pattern
Adopt the schedule, file the demand curves, and refresh the forecast each season

tasks.explanation: Production scheduling uses storage as the buffer between steady treatment and variable demand, and the schedule is judged on quality and storage together, not energy alone.

tasks.prompt: Order a bench to plant scale up study for a new coagulant product.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional plant in Manitoba evaluating a new coagulant for cold water performance.
tasks.configuration: Scope: bench screening through the plant scale decision filed.

cards.label: Run jar tests comparing the new and current products across temperature and raw quality ranges
Check alkalinity consumption, sludge production, and filtered quality for each product
Trial the leading product on one treatment train or in held plant steps for two weeks
Compare settled and filtered quality, filter runs, and sludge handling with the current product period
Confirm storage, feed compatibility, and delivered cost per treated volume for the new product
Decide adoption from the full comparison and file the study with the dose tables for both products

tasks.explanation: Scale up moves from bench to one train to the plant, and adoption weighs quality, sludge, and feed compatibility together, not bench turbidity alone.

tasks.prompt: Order a distribution water age and quality study fed by plant storage decisions.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in western Canada linking plant clearwell operation to distribution residual complaints.
tasks.configuration: Scope: age mapping through plant storage settings revised.

cards.label: Map storage volumes and turnover at the plant and in distribution reservoirs under current operation
Pair residual and temperature results with estimated water age at sample points
Identify where age, not plant dose, explains low residuals
Trial revised clearwell and reservoir level cycling to cut age at the worst points
Resample the same points and compare residuals at the new cycling pattern
Adopt the cycling settings and file the age study with the quality program

tasks.explanation: Low residuals are tested against water age before dose is raised, so storage cycling is corrected where age is the true cause.

tasks.prompt: Order a pilot plant study plan for a future membrane conversion.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional conventional plant in Alberta planning a pilot before a proposed membrane conversion.
tasks.configuration: Scope: pilot objectives set through pilot results ready for the capital decision.

cards.label: Set pilot objectives: sustainable flux, cleaning recovery, permeate quality, and waste volumes on the actual source
Size the pilot to run through the worst raw season, including cold and runoff conditions
Operate the pilot beside the existing plant on the same raw water with paired quality sampling
Log flux, pressure, cleaning, and chemical use in the same format the capital decision will use
Compare pilot permeate quality and residuals with the existing plant for the full pilot period
Report pilot results against each objective and file the data set for design use

tasks.explanation: A pilot earns its cost by running through the worst season on the real source, with results recorded in the exact form the design decision needs.

tasks.prompt: Order a treatment capacity study for a growing service population.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in British Columbia assessing when plant capacity will be reached.
tasks.configuration: Scope: rated capacities verified through the capacity trigger plan filed.

cards.label: Verify the true capacity of each process unit from records, testing, and condition, not nameplate alone
Compare unit capacities to find the limiting unit at current and forecast demands
Build demand forecasts from population growth and per capita use trends
Calculate the year each unit reaches its limit at the forecast growth rates
Stage capacity projects so the limiting unit is relieved before its trigger year
File the capacity study and set annual demand and capacity review dates

tasks.explanation: Capacity is set by the limiting unit at verified capacity, and projects are staged to its trigger year rather than to the plant nameplate.

tasks.prompt: Order a chemical feed system capacity and redundancy review.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Class 3 plant in Saskatchewan reviewing chemical feed reliability for critical chemicals.
tasks.configuration: Scope: critical chemical list through redundancy gaps closed or scheduled.

cards.label: List critical chemicals and the quality failure that follows if each feed stops
Check storage days on hand at peak dose and the delivery lead time for each chemical
Verify duty and standby feed equipment and test automatic or manual changeover for each system
Run each standby pump under load and confirm calibration matches the duty pump
Correct changeover or calibration defects and schedule any missing redundancy into the capital plan
File the review with days on hand triggers for reordering each chemical

tasks.explanation: Feed redundancy is proven by running standby equipment under load, and storage triggers are set from peak dose and lead time, not from average use.

tasks.prompt: Order an instrument reliability study for critical process analyzers.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional plant in Manitoba where analyzer outages have repeatedly forced manual control.
tasks.configuration: Scope: outage history through reliability improvements verified.

cards.label: Total analyzer outage hours and causes for turbidity, chlorine, pH, and flow instruments for one year
Rank analyzers by outage impact on control and on compliance records
Correct the top causes, such as sample line fouling, reagent supply, or spare parts gaps
Set preventive maintenance and calibration intervals from the corrected failure pattern
Track outage hours for the next quarter and compare with the study baseline
File the reliability program and stock the critical spares list it identifies

tasks.explanation: Analyzer reliability is fixed at its top measured causes, and success is judged by outage hours in the following quarter, not by the work orders closed.

tasks.prompt: Order a residuals production forecasting program for lagoon planning.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional plant in Alberta forecasting sludge production to plan lagoon capacity.
tasks.configuration: Scope: production factors set through the forecast adopted for lagoon planning.

cards.label: Calculate residuals factors from raw solids, chemical doses, and measured sludge production for one year
Reconcile the factors against lagoon level surveys and hauled volumes for the same year
Build monthly production forecasts from forecast flows and seasonal raw quality
Compare forecast lagoon filling with surveyed capacity and identify the year each cell fills
Schedule cell rotation, drying, and removal work ahead of the forecast fill dates
Update the forecast annually with the new production factors and file it with the residuals program

tasks.explanation: The forecast is reconciled to surveyed lagoon levels before it is trusted, so cell work is scheduled from measured filling, not from factors alone.

tasks.prompt: Order a lagoon cell rotation and drying program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional residuals lagoon system in Saskatchewan with three cells at different fill stages.
tasks.configuration: Scope: cell condition survey through the rotation program in service.

cards.label: Survey sludge depth and supernatant quality in every cell and record remaining capacity
Take the fullest cell out of service for drying while the remaining cells carry production
Manage supernatant return to the plant inlet at a controlled share with quality checks
Turn or harvest dried sludge when it reaches the program handling condition
Sample dried residuals for the approved disposal or beneficial use route before removal
Return the emptied cell to service and record the new rotation order and dates

tasks.explanation: Rotation rests one cell at a time while capacity is proven on the others, and dried material is sampled before it leaves by any route.

tasks.prompt: Order a residuals dewatering trial for mechanical thickening.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional plant in Manitoba trialing mechanical dewatering to replace lagoon drying.
tasks.configuration: Scope: trial objectives through the dewatering decision filed.

cards.label: Characterize sludge solids, production pattern, and current lagoon handling cost and capacity
Set trial measures: cake solids, capture rate, polymer use, and filtrate quality
Run the trial unit on representative sludge for at least two full production weeks
Check filtrate return impact on plant inlet quality during the trial
Compare trial results and full operating cost with the lagoon program
Decide adoption or return to lagoon handling from the evidence and file the trial report

tasks.explanation: The trial is judged on cake, capture, and filtrate together over representative weeks, because a dry cake with poor capture only moves the problem back to the inlet.

tasks.prompt: Order a backwash waste equalization and return program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional conventional plant in British Columbia returning settled backwash water to the inlet.
tasks.configuration: Scope: waste pattern measured through controlled return in routine service.

cards.label: Measure backwash waste volume and turbidity profile across representative washes
Size equalization use so return flow is steady and small compared with raw flow
Settle waste and return only supernatant that meets the program turbidity limit
Trial the return during stable raw quality and watch settled and filtered quality closely
Stop the return automatically on high waste turbidity or a raw water event
Adopt the program with return limits and record recovered volume in the water balance

tasks.explanation: Returned waste is settled, limited, and steady, with automatic stops for poor waste or raw events, so recovery never shocks the treatment it feeds.

tasks.prompt: Order a residuals disposal compliance and sampling program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in western Canada preparing lagoon sludge for its approved disposal route under provincial requirements in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: disposal requirements confirmed through sampled material released for removal.

cards.label: Confirm the sampling and quality requirements for the approved disposal route before any removal is booked
Sample each cell or stockpile on the required pattern and hold material until results are received
Compare results with the route limits and segregate any material that does not qualify
Book removal only for qualified material and record volumes, dates, and destination
Keep chain of custody and result records with the residuals file for each load
Review the program after each removal campaign and update the sampling pattern if the route changes

tasks.explanation: Material is sampled and qualified before removal is booked, and unqualified material is segregated rather than blended into a load.

tasks.prompt: Order a sludge blanket and residuals inventory control program for clarifiers.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional plant in Alberta linking clarifier blanket control to residuals receiving capacity.
tasks.configuration: Scope: receiving capacity set through blanket control matched to that capacity.

cards.label: Measure residuals tank and lagoon receiving capacity available each week
Set clarifier withdrawal volumes that the receiving system can actually accept
Sequence withdrawals across clarifiers so receiving capacity is never exceeded in one shift
Check sludge solids so watery withdrawals do not consume capacity without moving solids
Review blanket depths and receiving levels together at the weekly operations meeting
Adjust the withdrawal plan seasonally as residuals production and drying change

tasks.explanation: Clarifier withdrawal is paced by real receiving capacity and sludge solids, so solids are moved steadily instead of surging a full residuals system.

tasks.prompt: Order a residuals supernatant quality management program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional plant in Saskatchewan where lagoon supernatant returns have caused inlet quality upsets.
tasks.configuration: Scope: supernatant pattern studied through return rules adopted.

cards.label: Sample supernatant for turbidity, organics indicator, algae, and manganese across seasons
Relate plant upsets to supernatant return timing and share of raw flow
Set return quality limits and a maximum return share for each season
Add equalization or holding so returns avoid the plant during sensitive treatment periods
Trial the rules through one high risk season and track inlet quality during returns
Adopt the return rules in the residuals program and review them after each season

tasks.explanation: Supernatant is treated as a second raw source with its own limits and seasons, and return rules are proven through the high risk season before adoption.

tasks.prompt: Order a filter to waste and ripening water management program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional plant in Manitoba managing filter to waste volumes after backwashing.
tasks.configuration: Scope: ripening profiles measured through the waste program adopted.

cards.label: Profile effluent turbidity after backwash for every filter type and record time to target quality
Set filter to waste duration from the longest representative profile, not the average
Route filter to waste water to the residuals or recovery system sized for the peak volume
Trial a shortened waste period on one filter with continuous turbidity proof
Adopt the proven duration for each filter type and record it in the wash sequence
Trend waste volumes and effluent quality together in the monthly review

tasks.explanation: Filter to waste time is set from measured ripening profiles and shortened only on continuous turbidity proof, balancing water saving against effluent risk.

tasks.prompt: Order a residuals handling winter program for frozen lagoon conditions.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional residuals system in northern Alberta operating through frozen winter months.
tasks.configuration: Scope: winter capacity confirmed through winter withdrawal and storage settings in service.

cards.label: Survey usable lagoon and tank capacity before freeze up and calculate winter production
Confirm total winter storage can hold production until spring drying and hauling resume
Adjust clarifier withdrawal and sludge solids targets to make best use of winter storage
Protect transfer lines, valves, and pumps from freezing and test heat tracing before cold weather
Monitor levels monthly under ice using the winter measurement method
File the winter plan and the spring start up sequence for the residuals system

tasks.explanation: Winter planning proves storage can hold a full season of production before freeze up, because midwinter options are limited to what was prepared in the fall.

tasks.prompt: Order a chemical sludge conditioning program ahead of hauling.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional plant in western Canada conditioning lagoon sludge to cut hauled volume.
tasks.configuration: Scope: sludge condition assessed through conditioned material hauled and accounted.

cards.label: Measure sludge solids and volume in the cell or tank scheduled for hauling
Trial conditioning or gravity thickening on a measured batch and record solids gain and liquid released
Return released liquid to the plant under the supernatant return rules
Confirm conditioned solids meet the hauling and disposal route requirements
Haul the conditioned material and reconcile hauled volume with the starting inventory
Record the volume saved and update the residuals forecast factors

tasks.explanation: Conditioning is judged by reconciled volume saved and route compliance, with released liquid returned under the same rules as other supernatant.

tasks.prompt: Order a residuals program audit against production and disposal records.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional senior operator in British Columbia auditing three years of residuals records.
tasks.configuration: Scope: records gathered through audit findings assigned and closed.

cards.label: Gather production estimates, lagoon surveys, hauling records, and disposal receipts for the audit period
Reconcile solids produced, stored, and removed year by year and identify unexplained differences
Check sampling and disposal records for completeness against the program requirements
Investigate the largest reconciliation gap in the field by survey or measurement
Assign corrections for record, sampling, or handling gaps with owners and dates
Close the audit when records reconcile and file the audit with the residuals program

tasks.explanation: The audit reconciles produced, stored, and removed solids before judging paperwork, so a record gap is not mistaken for a handling gap, or the reverse.

tasks.prompt: Order a spent filter media inspection and replacement program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional plant in Saskatchewan planning media replacement across aging filters.
tasks.configuration: Scope: media condition assessed through replaced media verified in service.

cards.label: Core sample media from each filter and measure depth, grain condition, and fouling or mudball content
Rank filters by media condition and by effluent quality and run length evidence
Schedule replacement for the worst filter first during a low demand period with remaining filters proven
Remove spent media to the approved handling route and inspect underdrains while the filter is empty
Install new media to specification, wash and ripen the filter, and prove effluent quality before full service
Record new media baselines and set the inspection interval for the fleet

tasks.explanation: Media is replaced on core sample condition and performance evidence, underdrains are inspected while the filter is empty, and the renewed filter proves quality before full service.

tasks.prompt: Order a source water protection plan development for a river intake.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Alberta developing a source water protection plan for a prairie river intake.
tasks.configuration: Scope: source assessment through the adopted protection plan with assigned actions.

cards.label: Delineate the intake protection area using travel time and watershed mapping for the river reach
Inventory land uses and activities in the area that could affect raw water quality
Assess which activities pose the highest risk from likelihood, proximity, and intake sensitivity
Set protection actions with owners, such as setbacks, spill response links, and monitoring points
Establish raw water monitoring triggers that warn the plant before a quality change arrives
Adopt the plan with review dates and file it with the water quality management program

tasks.explanation: The plan moves from delineation to inventory to risk ranking, so protection actions and monitoring triggers are aimed at the highest risks first.

tasks.prompt: Order a watershed spill response readiness program for the intake.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional plant in Saskatchewan below highway, rail, and industrial crossings on its source river.
tasks.configuration: Scope: spill scenarios mapped through readiness proven by exercise.

cards.label: Map crossings and facilities upstream within the travel time window that matters for intake decisions
Confirm notification contacts and the information the plant needs: material, volume, location, and river condition
Set intake monitoring and shutdown triggers for the most likely spill materials
Stage sampling equipment and intake protection materials and confirm clearwell storage for a shutdown period
Run a tabletop exercise with operations staff using a realistic upstream spill timeline
Correct gaps found in contacts, triggers, or storage and file the readiness record

tasks.explanation: Readiness is proven by exercise against a travel time timeline, and shutdown triggers are set before an event, when there is time to think them through.

tasks.prompt: Order an algae and cyanobacteria seasonal monitoring program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional reservoir plant in Manitoba with summer algae blooms affecting treatment and taste.
tasks.configuration: Scope: bloom season baseline through treatment triggers adopted.

cards.label: Set the seasonal sampling schedule for algae indicators, raw taste and odour indicators, and reservoir conditions
Sample the reservoir at intake depth and at surface points where blooms accumulate
Relate bloom indicators to coagulant demand, filter runs, and treated taste results as the season builds
Set treatment triggers for oxidant or carbon use and for intake depth changes where available
Apply triggers during the peak bloom and record treatment response and customer complaints
Review the season and revise triggers and sampling points before the next bloom season

tasks.explanation: Bloom triggers are built from the plant own record linking indicators to treatment effects, so action starts on measurement, not on complaints.

tasks.prompt: Order a source monitoring program redesign after repeated raw quality surprises.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional plant in British Columbia whose intake monitoring missed several raw quality events.
tasks.configuration: Scope: missed events reviewed through the redesigned program proven on the next event.

cards.label: Review each missed event: what changed, when the plant learned of it, and what earlier signal existed
Add or move monitoring points so the earliest reliable signal is captured, including upstream points where justified
Set sampling frequency from river travel time so an event cannot pass between samples undetected
Link each new signal to a plant action, such as a jar test, dose review, or intake change
Run the redesigned program through the next raw event and compare warning time with the old program
Adopt the program and file the event comparison with the source protection plan

tasks.explanation: Redesign starts from the signals that existed but were not captured, and the new program is judged by warning time on the next real event.

tasks.prompt: Order a groundwater source protection and wellhead program for a well field.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional well field in Alberta supplying a growing town from several production wells.
tasks.configuration: Scope: well capture zones through protection actions in place.

cards.label: Delineate wellhead protection areas from pumping rates, aquifer information, and time of travel mapping
Inventory activities in the areas, including fuel storage, septic systems, and chemical handling
Rank risks and confirm which activities need agreements, relocation, or added monitoring
Install or schedule monitoring wells or sampling points between the highest risks and the production wells
Set raw well sampling that would detect a change early enough to take a well out of service
Adopt the program with land use contacts, review dates, and well response triggers

tasks.explanation: Wellhead protection ranks activities inside capture zones and places monitoring where it gives time to respond, not merely where sampling is easy.

tasks.prompt: Order the response plan for a raw water contamination warning from the province.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional plant in western Canada receiving a provincial advisory of a possible contaminant upstream, under provincial drinking water requirements in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: warning received through the plant returned to normal source use.

cards.label: Confirm the warning details with the issuing contact: contaminant, location, timing, and advice given
Increase raw sampling for the contaminant indicator and related general quality measures
Assess intake options: continue, reduce, close the intake and run on storage, or use an alternate source
Prepare treatment adjustments that the contaminant and plant processes support and brief all shifts
Decide intake action from sampling results and storage time available, and notify utility leadership
Return to normal intake use only on results that meet the advisory clearance and file the event record

tasks.explanation: The response confirms the warning first, samples for evidence, and weighs intake action against real storage time, so the decision is timed rather than rushed or delayed.

tasks.prompt: Order a multi barrier source to tap review for the whole system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Class 3 utility in Saskatchewan reviewing every barrier from watershed to customer tap.
tasks.configuration: Scope: barrier inventory through gaps assigned in the quality program.

cards.label: List each barrier in order: source protection, treatment, disinfection, storage, distribution, and monitoring
For each barrier, record what it removes or prevents and the evidence that it is working
Identify barriers that depend on a single piece of equipment, test, or person
Rank gaps by the quality risk if that barrier failed without warning
Assign strengthening actions, such as added monitoring, redundancy, or revised procedures, with dates
File the review in the water quality management program and set the annual review date

tasks.explanation: The review tests each barrier on evidence and single points of failure, so strengthening goes to the barrier whose silent failure would matter most.

tasks.prompt: Order an intake management program for frazil ice and winter blockage risk.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional river plant in northern Manitoba facing frazil ice that can block intake screens.
tasks.configuration: Scope: winter risk assessed through the intake program proven in cold weather.

cards.label: Review past blockage events for river temperature, flow, weather, and screen condition at the time
Install or verify river temperature and intake differential monitoring that warns before blockage
Set operator actions at each warning stage, including flow reduction and screen cleaning or backflushing
Confirm alternate capacity from storage or a second intake for a full blockage period
Trial the warning stages during the first cold snap and record whether warning time was adequate
File the winter intake program and stage spare parts and access equipment before each winter

tasks.explanation: Frazil ice gives short warning, so the program is built on temperature and differential signals with staged actions rehearsed before the coldest water arrives.

tasks.prompt: Order a drought source management program for a low reservoir year.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Alberta entering a dry year with a low reservoir and competing demands.
tasks.configuration: Scope: supply outlook through drought operating settings adopted.

cards.label: Build the supply outlook from reservoir level, snowpack and inflow records, and demand forecast
Set staged triggers tied to storage level for demand measures and plant operating changes
Confirm alternate or emergency source options and the quality treatment each would need
Adjust plant operation for the expected poorer raw quality at low reservoir levels
Communicate the stages and triggers to utility leadership and major users before they are reached
Review storage weekly through the dry season and file the drought record at season end

tasks.explanation: Drought stages are tied to measured storage with triggers set in advance, so demand and treatment changes happen on plan rather than in crisis.

tasks.prompt: Order a spring runoff preparedness program for a mountain river source.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional plant in British Columbia on a mountain river with rapid turbidity rises during runoff.
tasks.configuration: Scope: runoff forecast through the plant ready before the first major rise.

cards.label: Review past runoff records for peak turbidity, duration, and the speed of the fastest rise
Stage chemical inventories, sludge capacity, and filter availability for the runoff period
Pre run jar tests across the expected turbidity and colour range and post a runoff dose table
Brief all shifts on runoff triggers for dose changes, loading reductions, and added sampling
Confirm residuals capacity can accept the higher solids load of the runoff weeks
File the preparedness checklist and set the post runoff review date

tasks.explanation: Runoff readiness stages chemicals, residuals room, and a pre tested dose table before the rise, because the fastest events leave no time to prepare during them.

tasks.prompt: Order a drinking water quality management program annual review.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Class 3 utility in Alberta reviewing its quality management program for the year, in general alignment with provincial drinking water requirements.
tasks.configuration: Scope: program records gathered through revised program elements adopted.

cards.label: Gather the year records: quality results, incidents, audits, corrective actions, and customer complaints
Check each program element against its own procedures and record where practice differed from the written program
Review whether corrective actions from incidents were completed and effective
Identify the top quality risks for the coming year from the evidence reviewed
Revise procedures, monitoring, or training where the review shows a gap and assign owners and dates
Adopt the revised program, brief operating staff, and file the review record

tasks.explanation: The annual review compares practice with the written program element by element, and revisions are assigned from evidence, not from habit.

tasks.prompt: Order a corrective action program for a repeated adverse quality result.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Saskatchewan with the same distribution quality parameter failing in three separate months.
tasks.configuration: Scope: pattern confirmed through corrective action verified effective.

cards.label: Gather all results, sampling records, and plant and distribution conditions for the three events
Check sampling and laboratory quality first to rule out a measurement or handling cause
Trace the common operating condition across the events, such as storage age, dose, or a specific zone
Correct the common cause and set interim monitoring at the affected points
Verify effectiveness with a defined run of passing results at the same points
Close the corrective action only on the verification run and file the full record

tasks.explanation: A repeated result is treated as a system pattern, measurement is cleared first, and the action closes only on a defined run of passing results.

tasks.prompt: Order a sampling program design for a growing distribution system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Manitoba adding new subdivisions and a second pressure zone.
tasks.configuration: Scope: sampling requirements reviewed through the expanded program in service.

cards.label: List the sampling required by provincial drinking water requirements in general terms for the new system size and zones
Map existing sample points against population, zones, storage, and known dead ends
Add points so every zone and storage outlet is represented and high age areas are covered
Set the sampling calendar so required counts are met evenly through each period
Train samplers on the new points and update chain of custody and location records
Run the expanded program for one full period and audit result completeness before filing it as routine

tasks.explanation: New points are placed by zone, storage, and water age, and the expanded program is audited for completeness over a full period before it is trusted.

tasks.prompt: Order a laboratory quality assurance program for in house bench testing.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional plant laboratory in British Columbia performing the bench tests used for process control.
tasks.configuration: Scope: test list defined through routine quality checks trended.

cards.label: List every bench test used for control or reporting and the decision each result drives
Set calibration, blank, duplicate, and standard check requirements for each test
Run a comparison round where operators test shared samples and results are compared
Correct method or technique gaps found in the comparison and update bench method sheets
Trend duplicate and standard recoveries on control charts with action limits
File the quality program and schedule the next comparison round

tasks.explanation: Bench quality is proven by shared sample comparisons and trended checks, so a control decision never rests on a test whose accuracy is unknown.

tasks.prompt: Order an incident investigation and reporting program for treatment upsets.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Class 3 plant in western Canada standardizing how treatment upsets are investigated.
tasks.configuration: Scope: upset defined through the investigation closed with actions.

cards.label: Record the upset timeline from first abnormal signal to restored quality using control and log records
Secure samples and bench results from the upset period before they are discarded
Interview operators on each affected shift while the event is fresh and record their observations
Separate the initiating cause from contributing conditions, such as alarms, staffing, or equipment state
Assign corrective actions for the cause and the contributors with owners and dates
Verify the actions at the next similar condition and file the investigation

tasks.explanation: The investigation secures samples and timelines first, separates cause from contributors, and verifies actions at the next similar condition rather than on paper.

tasks.prompt: Order a customer complaint investigation program for taste and odour.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Alberta handling seasonal taste and odour complaints.
tasks.configuration: Scope: complaint intake standardized through the seasonal review completed.

cards.label: Record each complaint with location, time, description, and the water age and zone for the address
Sample at the complaint location and at upstream points for residual, temperature, and taste indicators
Compare complaint clusters with plant treated quality and distribution conditions for the same days
Act on the pattern found, such as flushing, storage cycling, or a plant treatment trigger
Contact complainants with the finding and the action taken once results are confirmed
Review the season complaints as a group and revise plant triggers or flushing plans

tasks.explanation: Complaints become evidence when each one carries location, age, and paired samples, and the season review turns the pattern into revised triggers.

tasks.prompt: Order a regulatory inspection readiness program for the treatment plant.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional plant in Saskatchewan preparing for a provincial drinking water inspection in general terms.
tasks.configuration: Scope: inspection scope reviewed through the plant ready with records organized.

cards.label: List the records an inspector will expect: approvals, monitoring results, calibration, training, and incident files
Check each record set for completeness and correct gaps in filing before filling any content gap
Walk the plant with the operations checklist and correct housekeeping, labelling, and access issues
Brief operators on likely questions about process control, alarms, and adverse result duties
Run a mock review of one month of results and trace every flagged value to its action record
File the readiness checklist and keep the organized records as the standing inspection file

tasks.explanation: Readiness traces flagged results to their action records, because an inspector follows exactly that path through the plant files.

tasks.prompt: Order a records and data integrity program for operating data.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Manitoba strengthening the reliability of its operating records.
tasks.configuration: Scope: record types inventoried through integrity checks in routine use.

cards.label: Inventory operating records by type, owner, retention need, and where each is stored
Set rules for corrections so original entries remain readable and changes carry date and author
Check a sample of electronic trends against bench sheets and logbooks for agreement
Correct the causes of disagreement, such as sensor mapping errors or missed manual entries
Back up electronic records on the program schedule and test restoring one record set
Adopt the integrity checks as a quarterly routine and file the program

tasks.explanation: Data integrity is proven by cross checking electronic trends against bench records and by a tested restore, not by the existence of a backup schedule alone.

tasks.prompt: Order an asset condition assessment program for critical treatment equipment.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Class 3 utility in Alberta assessing condition of pumps, blowers, chemical systems, and instruments.
tasks.configuration: Scope: critical asset list through condition based renewal priorities set.

cards.label: List critical assets by the service failure that follows if each one stops
Inspect each asset for condition, performance, maintenance history, and spare parts availability
Score condition and consequence together to rank renewal urgency
Check ranked assets against remaining life estimates and recent failure records
Place the top renewals in the capital and maintenance plans with years assigned
Set the reassessment interval and file the condition register

tasks.explanation: Renewal urgency ranks condition multiplied by consequence, so a poor condition asset that cannot stop the plant does not outrank a fair asset that can.

tasks.prompt: Order a capital project prioritization process for the treatment utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional utility in Saskatchewan choosing among membrane renewal, storage, chemical, and intake projects.
tasks.configuration: Scope: project list defined through the funded priority order adopted.

cards.label: Define each candidate project by the risk or capacity limit it addresses and the consequence of deferral
Score projects on public health risk, regulatory need, reliability, and capacity triggers in that order
Check each project for dependencies, such as storage needed before a plant outage project
Stage the funded order so health and regulatory projects lead and dependencies are respected
Record deferred projects with the trigger that will bring each one forward
Present the prioritized plan to utility leadership and file the scoring record

tasks.explanation: Prioritization scores health risk first and respects project dependencies, and deferred projects carry explicit triggers rather than being simply dropped.

tasks.prompt: Order a senior operator shift handover and decision log program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Class 3 plant in British Columbia formalizing handovers between senior operators.
tasks.configuration: Scope: handover content defined through the program audited for quality.

cards.label: Define the standing handover content: process state, quality results, equipment out of service, and pending decisions
Require the outgoing operator to record the reason and expected result for every dose or set point change
Hold a face to face or voice handover for any active upset, alarm watch, or unusual operation
Have the incoming operator read back critical items and confirm understanding before taking charge
Audit a sample of handovers monthly against plant events to find missed information
Revise the handover format from audit findings and file the program

tasks.explanation: Handovers carry reasons and expected results, not just settings, and monthly audits against real events keep the format honest.

tasks.prompt: Order the emergency response leadership sequence for a major plant failure.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional senior operator in Manitoba leading the response to a major treatment failure with storage falling.
tasks.configuration: Scope: failure declared through the recovery reviewed and filed.

cards.label: Declare the emergency, take command of the response, and assign operations, communications, and logistics roles
Protect public health first: stop or divert affected water and confirm storage and alternate supply status
Notify utility leadership and the provincial contact as provincial requirements direct in general terms
Direct the technical recovery in staged steps with quality checks before each return to service
Keep a timed decision log of conditions, actions, and notifications through the event
Lead the post event review, assign corrective actions, and file the full record

tasks.explanation: Command, public health protection, and notification come before technical recovery, and the timed log makes the later review a matter of record, not memory.

tasks.prompt: Order a cold climate plant wide winterization program at scale.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional large plant in northern Alberta winterizing treatment, residuals, and chemical systems together.
tasks.configuration: Scope: winter risk register through winter readiness verified before freeze up.

cards.label: Build a winter risk register covering intakes, basins, chemical storage, lines, residuals, and access
Inspect and test heat tracing, building heat, and backup power for every registered item
Set cold operating settings: loading, flux, dose verification frequency, and sludge handling changes
Stage winter spares, fuels, and chemicals for the period when deliveries are least reliable
Run a freeze failure drill on one critical system and correct the gaps it exposes
Sign off winter readiness by system and file the register with monthly winter check dates

tasks.explanation: Winterization is signed off system by system against a risk register and proven by a drill, so no critical system enters winter on assumption.

tasks.prompt: Order a freeze recovery sequence for a frozen chemical feed system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional plant in Saskatchewan where a coagulant feed line froze overnight in extreme cold.
tasks.configuration: Scope: feed loss confirmed through feed restored and cold protection upgraded.

cards.label: Confirm the feed loss by drawdown and switch to the standby feed path or alternate chemical arrangement
Protect treated quality by reducing plant flow to what the available feed can treat correctly
Thaw the frozen line and fittings gradually with the approved method and inspect for cracks or leaks
Flush and pressure check the repaired line and recalibrate the feed by drawdown
Restore normal flow in steps as feed delivery and settled quality are proven
Upgrade insulation and heat tracing on the failed section and record the event in the winter register

tasks.explanation: Quality is protected by cutting flow to what available feed can treat, the line is proven by pressure check and drawdown, and the cold protection fix closes the event.

tasks.prompt: Order a staffing and competency program for senior operator coverage.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional regional utility in western Canada ensuring qualified senior coverage on every shift.
tasks.configuration: Scope: coverage requirement defined through the competency program in routine use.

cards.label: Define the senior tasks that must be covered on each shift, including upset response and regulatory duties in general terms
Assess each operator against the task list using records, exercises, and supervised performance
Build development plans for gaps, pairing operators with mentors on the tasks they lack
Schedule coverage so no shift depends on a single person for a critical task
Reassess after the development period and update the coverage matrix
File the competency program and review it when processes or regulations change

tasks.explanation: Coverage is built from a task list and assessed performance, and the schedule is tested so no critical task rests on one person.

tasks.prompt: Order a management of change process for a treatment process modification.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional plant in Alberta changing its disinfection arrangement and chemical feed points.
tasks.configuration: Scope: change proposed through the change closed after proven operation.

cards.label: Describe the change, its reason, and every process, safety, and record it will affect
Review the change for quality risks, including interim operation while work proceeds
Update procedures, dose tables, alarms, and training before the change is made
Make the change under a planned outage or controlled condition with quality checks staged
Operate under heightened monitoring for a defined proving period and compare results with the change goals
Close the change only when goals are met and all updated documents are in use

tasks.explanation: Documents and training are updated before the change is made, and closure waits for a proving period, so the plant never runs a new process on old instructions.

tasks.prompt: Order a budget and chemical inventory planning cycle for the operating year.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Class 3 utility in Manitoba planning chemical purchasing for price and supply security.
tasks.configuration: Scope: use forecast built through the purchasing plan adopted.

cards.label: Forecast chemical use from production forecast, dose tables, and seasonal quality patterns
Set minimum and maximum stock levels from delivery lead times, storage life, and outage risk
Schedule bulk deliveries to respect storage capacity and seasonal access limits
Compare suppliers on delivered cost, reliability, and product quality record
Place contracts or orders for the year with the stock triggers written into the plan
Review use against forecast quarterly and adjust orders before stock limits are threatened

tasks.explanation: Purchasing is planned from forecast use and lead time risk, with stock triggers set so supply security does not depend on one operator memory.

tasks.prompt: Transmembrane pressure on ultrafiltration Train 1 at a Saskatchewan plant has climbed steadily for three weeks at constant flux, while Train 2 on the same feed is stable.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 3 water treatment plant case for study: records, bench tests and paired comparisons described are available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: Train 1 transmembrane pressure rose from 55 kPa to 110 kPa at a constant flux of 45 L per square metre per hour.
Train 2, fed from the same header, held near 58 kPa over the same period.
A chemically enhanced backwash on Train 1 recovers only about 10 percent of the pressure rise, and the next rise starts within hours.
Pretreated feed turbidity, temperature corrected permeability checks and feed pressure are all in their usual ranges.
A removed fibre bundle sample from Train 1 shows a thick slimy coating that smears when touched.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: Biofouling is building up on Train 1 membranes and is not being removed by the routine backwash
Feed water turbidity has risen and is overloading both trains
The Train 1 pressure transmitter has drifted high
Cold feed water has raised viscosity across the whole plant

inference.explanation: Only Train 1 is affected on a shared feed, which rules out feed quality, viscosity and a plant wide cause. A transmitter drift would not leave a slimy coating on the fibres or respond partly to chemical backwash. The coating and the fast return of pressure point to biofilm growth.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record or check best confirms the explanation?

options.label: Archived normalized permeability and cleaning recovery trends for both trains
Archived feed pump discharge pressure log
Archived raw water temperature log

nextClue.explanation: Archived normalized permeability and cleaning recovery trends for both trains directly tests or records the condition behind the keyed explanation, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Trends show Train 1 permeability falling week over week with shrinking recovery after each clean, while Train 2 stayed flat, the classic biofouling pattern.
clueText.nc-b: Feed pump pressure was steady, which does not separate one train from the other.
clueText.nc-c: Raw temperature changed little over the three weeks and affected both trains equally.

tasks.prompt: Membrane flux at a Manitoba ultrafiltration plant must be cut back every few days to hold transmembrane pressure, and each chemical clean restores less than the last.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 3 water treatment plant case for study: records, bench tests and paired comparisons described are available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: Normalized permeability has fallen about 30 percent over two months despite weekly chemical cleans.
Recovery after cleaning fell from 95 percent of baseline to 78 percent over the same period.
Feed water iron measures 0.6 mg/L, well above the membrane supplier guideline of 0.1 mg/L for this system.
The upstream oxidation and filtration step that removes iron has been bypassed for two months for repairs.
A membrane autopsy sample shows reddish brown deposits rich in iron.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: Membrane fibres are ageing normally and the loss is expected wear
Iron fouling from the bypassed pretreatment step is causing increasingly irreversible permeability loss
Air scour blowers are undersized for the current flux
The permeate flow meter reads low and flux is actually normal

inference.explanation: Iron in the feed is six times the supplier guideline, the iron removal step is bypassed, deposits are iron rich, and cleaning recovery keeps shrinking, which marks irreversible fouling. Normal ageing would not track the bypass period, and a meter error would not produce iron deposits.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record or check best confirms the explanation?

options.label: Archived air scour blower run hours
Archived feed iron results and pretreatment bypass log for the past two months
Archived permeate turbidity log

nextClue.explanation: Archived feed iron results and pretreatment bypass log for the past two months directly tests or records the condition behind the keyed explanation, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Blower hours were normal, and scour problems usually recover fully after a clean.
clueText.nc-b: Feed iron rose the week the pretreatment step was bypassed and stayed high, matching the start of the permeability decline.
clueText.nc-c: Permeate turbidity stayed low, which speaks to integrity, not fouling rate.

tasks.prompt: Permeate turbidity on one membrane rack at an Alberta plant spiked during a pressure decay test, and the rack was taken out of service.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 3 water treatment plant case for study: records, bench tests and paired comparisons described are available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: The pressure decay rate on Rack 3 is four times the rate on the other racks.
Sonic testing along Rack 3 localizes a strong signal to one module in the middle of the rack.
Permeate turbidity from Rack 3 rose to 0.28 NTU while other racks stayed near 0.04 NTU.
Feed turbidity and plant flow were steady during the test.
When the suspect module was isolated and the rack retested, the decay rate returned to the normal range.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The whole rack of membranes has reached end of life
The permeate turbidimeter needs calibration
A broken fibre or seal in the one suspect module is letting feed water pass into the permeate
Feed turbidity overwhelmed the rack during the test

inference.explanation: Decay is rack specific, sonic testing points to one module, and isolating that module restores the decay rate. End of life would affect the rack evenly, a meter fault would not change a pressure decay result, and feed conditions were steady.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record or check best confirms the explanation?

options.label: Archived turbidimeter calibration certificates
Archived membrane purchase records
Archived pressure decay test history for all racks

nextClue.explanation: Archived pressure decay test history for all racks directly tests or records the condition behind the keyed explanation, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Calibration was current, and the other racks read normally on the same instruments.
clueText.nc-b: Purchase records show the racks are mid life, not at end of life.
clueText.nc-c: Rack 3 decay was normal at the last quarterly test and jumped only this quarter, matching a discrete break rather than gradual ageing.

tasks.prompt: Reverse osmosis recovery at a British Columbia interior plant was raised from 75 percent to 85 percent, and within a month the tail elements began losing performance.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 3 water treatment plant case for study: records, bench tests and paired comparisons described are available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: Normalized permeate flow from the last stage fell 18 percent while first stage flow is unchanged.
Concentrate silica and calcium are near their solubility limits at the higher recovery.
Acid cleaning restores most of the last stage performance, and the cleaning solution carries heavy scale residue.
Feed pressure had to rise to hold total permeate production.
Antiscalant dose was not changed when recovery was raised.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: Biological fouling is blocking the tail elements
The membranes were damaged by chlorine in the feed
The feed pump is losing capacity
Scale is forming on the tail elements because the higher recovery pushed concentrate chemistry past solubility limits

inference.explanation: The loss is concentrated in the tail stage where concentrate is strongest, chemistry sits at solubility limits, acid cleaning restores flow and removes scale, and antiscalant was never adjusted. Biofouling usually hits the lead elements first, and chlorine damage would not be reversed by acid cleaning.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record or check best confirms the explanation?

options.label: Archived normalized stage performance and concentrate chemistry trends since the recovery change
Archived feed chlorine residual log
Archived lead element cleaning records

nextClue.explanation: Archived normalized stage performance and concentrate chemistry trends since the recovery change directly tests or records the condition behind the keyed explanation, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Stage trends show the decline began within days of the recovery increase and is confined to the last stage, matching the chemistry trend.
clueText.nc-b: Feed chlorine was non detectable throughout, which clears oxidant damage.
clueText.nc-c: Lead element records show stable performance, against a feed end fouling pattern.

tasks.prompt: A northern Saskatchewan membrane plant meets its flux target in summer but cannot hold production in January without exceeding its pressure limit.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 3 water treatment plant case for study: records, bench tests and paired comparisons described are available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: Raw water temperature is 1 C in January compared with 16 C in July.
Temperature corrected permeability is almost the same in January and July.
Available membrane area, cleaning state and feed quality are similar in both seasons.
Operators must raise transmembrane pressure about 70 percent in January to hold the same flux.
A pilot run at winter temperature in the lab needed the same pressure increase to hold flux.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: Cold water viscosity, not fouling, is raising the pressure needed to hold flux in winter
The membranes foul every winter because of algae
Ice is blocking part of the membrane area
The feed pumps lose efficiency in cold weather

inference.explanation: Temperature corrected permeability is unchanged, which means the membrane itself performs the same once viscosity is accounted for, and the lab pilot reproduces the effect with temperature alone. Fouling would lower corrected permeability, and no ice or pump evidence is offered.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record or check best confirms the explanation?

options.label: Archived algae counts for the source reservoir
Archived temperature corrected permeability trends across two full winters
Archived feed pump efficiency test results

nextClue.explanation: Archived temperature corrected permeability trends across two full winters directly tests or records the condition behind the keyed explanation, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Algae counts peak in summer, the opposite season to the problem.
clueText.nc-b: Corrected permeability stayed flat through both winters while raw pressure tracked temperature, confirming a viscosity effect.
clueText.nc-c: Pump tests show normal efficiency at winter temperatures.

tasks.prompt: Chemical cleaning costs at a prairie membrane plant have doubled in a year, and the senior operator is asked to find out why cleans are being triggered so often.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 3 water treatment plant case for study: records, bench tests and paired comparisons described are available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: Cleans are triggered on a fixed 14 day calendar schedule regardless of membrane condition.
Normalized permeability at the time of most cleans had fallen only 3 to 5 percent, well above the supplier trigger of 10 to 15 percent.
Membrane condition after a year of frequent cleaning shows early signs of chemical wear.
Feed quality records show long stable periods with no fouling challenge.
A trial train cleaned only on condition ran 41 days between cleans with no lasting permeability loss.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: Feed quality has worsened and truly needs more cleaning
Calendar based cleaning is being done far more often than membrane condition requires
The cleaning chemicals have lost strength
Operators are skipping backwashes, forcing extra cleans

inference.explanation: Permeability at clean time is barely below baseline, a condition based trial train ran nearly three times longer with no harm, and feed quality is stable. The trigger is the calendar, not the water, and chemical wear is appearing from the extra cleans themselves.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record or check best confirms the explanation?

options.label: Archived chemical delivery certificates
Archived backwash completion log
Archived clean trigger records with permeability at each clean for the past year

nextClue.explanation: Archived clean trigger records with permeability at each clean for the past year directly tests or records the condition behind the keyed explanation, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Delivery certificates show chemicals at full strength.
clueText.nc-b: Backwash completion was near complete all year.
clueText.nc-c: Records show most cleans fired on schedule at 3 to 5 percent loss, and the trial train record shows condition based cleaning held performance.

tasks.prompt: Permeate quality from a membrane plant in the Yukon deteriorated slowly over a season, with log removal credit questioned at the last provincial review.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 3 water treatment plant case for study: records, bench tests and paired comparisons described are available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: Direct integrity test results have crept upward for three quarters but remain just inside the pass limit.
Two modules show slightly elevated sonic responses that were noted and filed without follow up.
Permeate turbidity is still low at 0.05 NTU and shows no spikes.
Continuous indirect monitoring was relied on between quarterly direct tests.
When the two flagged modules were removed, fibres with pinhole damage were found in both.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The membranes are removing less because the pores have enlarged with age
The turbidity meter is reading low and hiding large leaks
Small fibre damage in the two flagged modules is growing and indirect monitoring alone missed its significance
Feed water pathogen load has increased beyond design

inference.explanation: Direct test creep, repeated sonic flags on the same two modules, and pinholes found in exactly those modules tie the trend to discrete damage. Low steady turbidity fits small leaks, and no feed load or meter evidence is offered.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record or check best confirms the explanation?

options.label: Archived direct integrity test trend and sonic survey records by module
Archived feed water quality summaries
Archived turbidimeter maintenance log

nextClue.explanation: Archived direct integrity test trend and sonic survey records by module directly tests or records the condition behind the keyed explanation, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: The trend shows the two modules flagged every survey while all others stayed flat, and removal confirmed the damage.
clueText.nc-b: Feed summaries show no step change in source quality.
clueText.nc-c: Meter maintenance is current and checks against a bench meter agree.

tasks.prompt: After a wildfire in the watershed, a membrane plant in British Columbia saw cleaning frequency triple and filterability of the feed collapse.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 3 water treatment plant case for study: records, bench tests and paired comparisons described are available for review, and provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality apply in general terms.

evidence.label: Raw water dissolved organic carbon doubled after the fire and ash runoff reached the intake.
A filterability index test on the feed fell to half its pre fire value.
Coagulation ahead of the membranes was still set for pre fire conditions and jar tests now show a higher optimum dose.
Membrane fouling layers are dark and organic in appearance.
Raising the coagulant dose in a pilot skid restored feed filterability close to pre fire values.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The fire damaged the membranes with heat through the intake water
Ash particles are physically plugging the membrane pores directly
The cleaning skid has failed and cleans are ineffective
Fire driven organic loading overwhelmed the pretreatment, and the fouled membranes are a symptom of under coagulated feed

inference.explanation: Organics doubled, filterability collapsed, jars show the pretreatment dose is now too low, and a pilot skid with corrected dose restores filterability. The fouling is organic and upstream driven, not heat or a cleaning skid fault.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record or check best confirms the explanation?

options.label: Archived cleaning skid maintenance log
Archived feed dissolved organic carbon, filterability and dose records since the fire
Archived intake water temperature log

evidence.label: Salt passage for the vessel rose from 2 percent to 7 percent over two weeks.
Probing the vessel shows one element position with conductivity far above its neighbours.
Vessel feed and concentrate pressures and total train recovery are unchanged.
A vacuum hold test on the suspect element fails while its neighbours pass.
Permeate flow from the vessel is slightly higher than expected for its feed pressure.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: A damaged seal or membrane defect in the one probed element is letting feed bypass into the permeate
The whole train is scaling and losing rejection
Feed conductivity rose and the vessel is only reflecting it
The conductivity meter cell is fouled

inference.explanation: The change is confined to one vessel and one element position, the element fails a vacuum hold test, and higher flow with worse quality fits a bypass. Scaling would affect the train and raise pressures, and feed conductivity is unchanged.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record or check best confirms the explanation?

options.label: Archived feed conductivity trend
Archived conductivity meter calibration record
Archived vessel probing profiles and element test records

clueText.nc-a: Feed conductivity was flat through the change.

clueText.nc-c: Probing history shows the same element position stepping up over two weeks while all other positions stayed flat.

A trial with pressure based triggering cut backwash count by half with no rise in average pressure over a month.
Feed turbidity is low and stable for most of the year.
Membrane permeability trends are healthy.

Timer based backwashing is running far more often than fouling requires, wasting treated water
Backwash valves are leaking production water to waste
The waste flow meter over reads

Archived waste meter calibration record
Archived valve inspection report

clueText.nc-a: Records show backwash count flat across seasons while pressure rise per cycle stayed small, and the trial section shows the saving directly.

clueText.nc-c: Valve inspections found no passing valves.

After screens are steamed clear, feed recovers within an hour with no other change.

The raw pumps are worn and cannot keep up

The feed tank level instrument reads low in cold weather

Disposal contractor rates alone explain the cost rise
The uncalibrated concentrate meter under reads, so disposal volumes and costs were misjudged from bad data

The lamps are ageing and losing output by afternoon heat
The UV intensity sensor drifts as the day warms up
Afternoon flows exceed the validated range

Lamp output measured independently matches the lamp specification.
Water transmittance records are normal for the source.

The fouled duty sensor over read intensity, so reported dose was overstated for a year
Transmittance was better than the records show
The reference sensor is the faulty instrument

Archived transmittance log

No fouling is found on sleeves during January inspections.

Cold water is suppressing lamp output below its rating, cutting delivered dose each winter
The plant exceeds validated flow every winter

Archived transmittance seasonal summary

Lamp output and transmittance during the test matched the validated conditions.
Dose measured by biodosimetry fell short only in the high flow run.

Transmittance dropped during the high flow run
The biodosimetry organism was unusually resistant in that run
